paragraphs: Among a democratic people, where there is no hereditary wealth, every man works to earn a living, or has worked, or was born to parents who worked. The idea of labor is therefore presented to the mind on every side as the necessary, natural, and honest condition of human existence. Among such a people labor is not only not dishonorable; it is held in honor. The prejudice is not against it but in its favor. In the United States, a wealthy man thinks he owes it to public opinion to devote his leisure to some industrial or commercial pursuit, or to public business. He would think himself in bad repute if he spent his life merely living. So many rich Americans come to Europe to escape this obligation to work. There they find some scattered remains of aristocratic society, among which idleness is still held in honor.

Equality of conditions not only ennobles the idea of labor in men’s estimation; it also raises the idea of labor as a source of profit. In aristocracies it is not exactly labor that is despised, but labor done for profit. Labor is honorable in itself when it is undertaken solely at the bidding of ambition or virtue. Yet in aristocratic society it constantly happens that a man who works for honor is not insensible to the attractions of profit. But these two desires mingle only in the innermost depths of his soul. He carefully hides from every eye the point where they join, and he would gladly hide it from himself. In aristocratic countries there are few public officials who do not pretend to serve their country without self-interested motives. Their salary is a detail they think little about and always pretend not to think about at all. In this way the idea of profit is kept distinct from that of labor. However closely they may be united in fact, they are not thought of together.

In democratic communities, by contrast, these two ideas are always plainly united. The desire for well-being is universal, fortunes are slender or fluctuating, and everyone wants either to increase his own resources or to provide new ones for his children. Men therefore see clearly that it is profit that leads them to work, if not wholly, at least in part. Even those who are driven chiefly by the love of fame are inevitably made familiar with the thought that fame is not their only motive. They find that the desire to earn a living is mixed in their minds with the desire to make life illustrious.

Once the whole community holds labor to be an honorable necessity of man’s condition, and once labor is always openly performed, wholly or in part, to earn pay, the immense distance that separated different callings in aristocratic societies disappears. If all are not alike, all at least have one feature in common. There is no profession in which men do not work for money, and the pay that is common to all gives them all an air of resemblance. This helps explain the opinions Americans hold about different callings. In America no one is degraded because he works, for everyone around him works too. Nor is anyone humiliated by the idea of receiving pay, for the President of the United States also works for pay. He is paid for giving orders, other men for obeying them. In the United States professions are more or less laborious and more or less profitable, but they are never high or low: every honest calling is honorable.
